title: The temple falls (AD 70)
hook: Rome destroys the temple, and both Judaism and Christianity must learn to live without it
carry: pray for the peace of jerusalem

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter and Paul in Rome, and your line was faithful to the end. What did you finish? Today, a loss that changed two faiths at once. Day seven hundred fifty-one.

Walking out of the temple in Jerusalem, the rebuilt temple that stood where the old one had burned, a disciple turns to Jesus, full of awe: "Master, see what manner of stones and what buildings are here!" Look at the size of these stones. And Jesus answers: "Seest thou these great buildings? there shall not be left one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down." In Mark's Gospel, it's said in passing, on the way out. Years later, Roman armies put down a revolt in Judaea, and the temple burns. The house of God in Jerusalem is gone. Jews and Christians both have to answer the same question: now what?

Start with grief, because the texts do. Luke says that when Jesus came near the city, "he beheld the city, and wept over it." He wept for Jerusalem, not against it. The temple was the center of Jewish worship: sacrifice, the festivals, the priests. For the first Christians, it was their temple too; Acts shows the apostles praying there day after day. When it fell, both communities had to find how God is worshiped without it. Jewish tradition tells of teachers who rebuilt Judaism around prayer, study and the home. A rabbinic story remembers a teacher walking past the ruins with a student who mourns that the place of atonement is gone. The teacher says there is another atonement as good: deeds of loving-kindness, and he quotes the prophet Hosea: "For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice." Christians know that verse too. In Matthew, Jesus quotes it twice. Jews still mourn the temple on a fast day, Tisha B'Av, and at a Jewish wedding, tradition breaks a glass to remember Jerusalem in the middle of joy. Christians, for their part, spoke of a temple that couldn't burn. John says that when Jesus said destroy this temple, "he spake of the temple of his body." And Paul writes to Corinth: "Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?" Two faiths, one loss, and some shared verses to carry it. And the city itself is still prayed for, in a psalm both Jews and Christians sing: "Pray for the peace of Jerusalem: they shall prosper that love thee."

Here's the practice: pray, or hope, for Jerusalem. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the city as it is today: Jews at the Western Wall, Christians in the old churches, Muslims at their mosque, families in ordinary streets, people who are afraid. Don't take a side for two minutes. Just hold all of them. If you pray, you can say the psalm's own line slowly, a few times: pray for the peace of Jerusalem. If you don't pray, hold the city in your attention and wish it peace. The bell holds the time.
The temple falls. Rome destroys the temple in Jerusalem, and both Jews and Christians learn to worship without it.
Your line: pray for the peace of jerusalem. Today, when you see a headline about the city, stop for one breath and wish it peace before you scroll on. Day seven hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Christians pray for Jerusalem with the words of Psalm 122, and the fall of the temple is read in churches from the Gospels, where Jesus foretells it and weeps over the city.

what it means: a shared loss that Jews and Christians both had to live through, and learn to worship after.
what a scholar hears: the shift from sacrifice to mercy, prayer and study, carried by Hosea 6:6, a verse both traditions keep.

notes: Editor pass: invented 'ordinary afternoon' and 'country boy' cut; 'a generation later' changed to 'years later' (no time span in the cited text); 'had already been speaking' cut because it implies a dating of John's Gospel; 'where heaven and earth were said to meet' cut; first myth item reworded so it doesn't overstate.

No year is stated in the voice under the claims rule; the title's 'AD 70' comes from the index. 'A generation later' and 'Roman armies put down a revolt in Judaea, and the temple burns' are general history; confirm.
'For the first Christians, who were mostly Jews' is a historical claim not in the cited text; Acts 2–3 support the apostles' temple prayer. The phrase about most early Christians being Jews was cut.

The rabbinic story (Avot de-Rabbi Natan 4: Yohanan ben Zakkai tells Rabbi Joshua that deeds of loving-kindness atone, citing Hosea 6:6) is paraphrased and attributed to 'a rabbinic story'. A Jewish reviewer should check the framing.
Tisha B'Av and the breaking of a glass at Jewish weddings 'to remember Jerusalem' are described as Jewish practice; Phrased as tradition; confirm.
The practice names Jews, Christians and Muslims in Jerusalem without taking a political side; confirm it is balanced.
Original: שַׁאֲלוּ שְׁלוֹם יְרוּשָׁלָםִ (Psalm 122:6). Confirm pointing and transliteration.
